lead: A horizontal angle fixes direction: it is what a traverse, a triangulation net and a building layout are built from. A vertical angle fixes slope: with a distance it gives a height. The theodolite reads both on graduated circles, and the way the readings are taken decides how many of the instrument's errors cancel. Reading both verniers removes eccentricity, observing on both faces removes collimation, trunnion-axis and index errors, and repeating the angle on different parts of the circle reduces graduation error.
prereq: You need: the parts of the theodolite, face left and face right, and the temporary adjustments from Theodolite: parts and adjustments.

sections.h3: Horizontal angle by the ordinary method

blocks.text: The horizontal angle PQR at station Q is the angle between the vertical planes through QP and QR; the theodolite measures it on the horizontal circle whatever the heights of P and R. The circle is graduated clockwise, so an angle is always measured by turning clockwise from the first station to the second.

items: Set up over Q and make the temporary adjustments. Work on face left.
With the upper clamp, set vernier A to 0°00′00″ and clamp. Release the lower clamp, sight P and bisect it with the lower tangent screw. Read both verniers.
Release the upper clamp, turn clockwise to R, clamp and bisect with the upper tangent screw. Read both verniers.
Angle = mean reading at R − mean reading at P. Vernier B reads 180° more; drop the 180° before averaging its minutes and seconds with those of A.
Change face and repeat on face right. The result is the mean of the two faces.

blocks.text: To read a vernier, take the degrees and minutes at the main-scale mark just before the vernier's zero, then find the vernier line that coincides with a main-scale line and add its value. On a 20″ instrument the vernier is figured in minutes and 20″ steps.

In the repetition method the angle is added on the circle several times without reading in between, and the total is divided by the number of repetitions. Readings accumulate on different parts of the circle, so graduation errors average out, and the vernier's least count is divided by n. The usual set is three repetitions on face left, then three on face right.

items: Set 0°00′00″, sight P with the lower clamp and lower tangent screw, read both verniers.
Release the upper clamp, sight R with the upper motion. This is the first repetition; a rough reading checks the total later.
Release the lower clamp (the reading stays on the circle), turn back to P and bisect with the lower motion.
Release the upper clamp, turn to R and bisect with the upper motion. The circle now shows twice the angle. Repeat until n repetitions; read both verniers.
Angle = (final mean reading − initial reading) ÷ n, adding 360° to the final reading for each complete turn of the circle.

blocks.text: In the direction method (reiteration), several stations A, B, C, D are sighted in turn clockwise from one reference, and the readings are booked as directions; each angle is the difference of two directions. The round ends on the reference again (closing the horizon). The closing error e (final reading − first reading, on a full circle) is shared equally among the m angles of the round, so the corrections to the directions are cumulative: 0 at the reference, −e/m at the first station, −2e/m at the next, and −e on the closing sight. The round is repeated on the other face and with the circle set to different starting values.

A vertical angle α is the angle between the line of sight and the horizontal in a vertical plane: an angle of elevation (positive) or depression (negative). The zenith distance z is measured from the vertical; α = 90° − z. Older vernier theodolites have a vertical circle reading 0°–90° in four quadrants, with the 0° at the horizontal; most electronic instruments read zenith distance from 0° to 360°.

Face left:  α<sub>L</sub> = 90° − z<sub>L</sub>;   face right:  α<sub>R</sub> = z<sub>R</sub> − 270°
α = ½(α<sub>L</sub> + α<sub>R</sub>);   index error = ½[(z<sub>L</sub> + z<sub>R</sub>) − 360°]
blocks.where: z<sub>L</sub>, z<sub>R</sub> are the zenith readings on face left and face right of the same point. On a perfect instrument z<sub>L</sub> + z<sub>R</sub> = 360°. The index error is subtracted from z<sub>L</sub> to correct a single face-left reading.

blocks.text: To observe, centre the altitude bubble (or let the compensator settle), bisect the point with the horizontal hair on face left, read the vertical circle, then repeat on face right. The mean of the faces removes the index error and the error of an altitude level not parallel to the line of sight.

examples.question: With a 20″ theodolite at Q, the angle PQR is measured by three repetitions on each face, starting from 0°00′00″ on P. After three repetitions the verniers read: face left, A 128°33′40″ and B 308°34′20″; face right, A 128°34′40″ and B 308°35′20″. Find the angle on each face and the final angle.
steps: Face left: drop the 180° from vernier B, so B gives 128°34′20″. Mean of the verniers = ½(128°33′40″ + 128°34′20″) = 128°34′00″.

The faces differ by 20″, small enough for a 20″ instrument used three times (each repetition result is read to 20″ ÷ 3 ≈ 7″); a difference of a minute or more would mean a slipped clamp or a bad bisection.
examples.answer: Face left 42°51′20″, face right 42°51′40″; the angle PQR = 42°51′30″.

examples.question: A theodolite with a zenith-reading vertical circle sights the top of a mast. Face left reads 84°12′40″ and face right reads 275°47′40″. Find the vertical angle, the index error, and the corrected face-left reading.
steps: Check by the sum: z<sub>L</sub> + z<sub>R</sub> = 84°12′40″ + 275°47′40″ = 360°00′20″. Index error = ½(20″) = +10″.
Corrected face-left zenith reading = 84°12′40″ − 10″ = 84°12′30″, giving α = 90° − 84°12′30″ = 5°47′30″, the same as the face mean.
examples.answer: Vertical angle +5°47′30″ (elevation); index error +10″; corrected face-left zenith distance 84°12′30″.

traps: Averaging vernier B without dropping 180°. B reads about 180° more than A; only its minutes and seconds are averaged with A.
Dividing by n without subtracting the initial reading, or forgetting the 360° added each time the circle passes zero in repetition.
Applying the same correction to every direction after closing the horizon. The corrections grow step by step, from 0 at the reference to −e at the closing sight.
Taking a zenith reading as the vertical angle. α = 90° − z on face left; a z above 90° means a depression.
Expecting changing face to remove the error of a vertical axis that is not vertical, or refraction. Neither reverses with the face.

quiz.q: Define a horizontal angle, a vertical angle and a zenith distance.
quiz.a: Horizontal angle: the angle between the vertical planes through the two lines of sight, measured in the horizontal plane. Vertical angle: the angle between a line of sight and the horizontal, in a vertical plane, positive up. Zenith distance: the angle from the vertical (zenith) to the line of sight; α = 90° − z.

quiz.q: Why is the lower clamp released when the telescope is turned back to the first station in the repetition method?
quiz.a: With the lower clamp free and the upper clamp locked, the circle turns with the telescope, so the reading already on it is carried back to the first station unchanged. The next upper-motion turn then adds the angle again on top of it.

quiz.q: A round of directions starts at 0°00′00″ on A, reads B, C and D, and closes on A at 0°00′24″. State the corrections.
quiz.a: e = +24″ over m = 4 angles, so 6″ per angle. Corrections: A 0, B −6″, C −12″, D −18″, closing A −24″.

quiz.q: A zenith-reading theodolite gives 96°18′20″ on face left and 263°41′20″ on face right for a point. Find the vertical angle and the index error.
An angle measured once on each face gives 72°15′40″ and 72°16′20″. A second set by six repetitions gives 72°16′05″. Which value would you adopt, and why?
quiz.a: The repetition value, 72°16′05″, or a weighted mean leaning towards it. The single-face values carry the full least count error and one graduation error each; six repetitions spread the reading over the circle and divide the reading error by six. The 40″ gap between the single faces also suggests a bisection or clamp slip.

quiz.q: Is the repetition method or the direction method better at a triangulation station with five stations to be observed? Justify.
quiz.a: The direction method. With five stations, repetition must measure each angle separately, which is slow and repeats each pointing many times. The direction method observes all five in one round, gives every angle from two directions, checks itself by closing the horizon, and is repeated on both faces with different initial settings to beat graduation error.

beyond: Not for the exam. Electronic theodolites read angles to 1″ or better and store directions in sets, so the direction method on both faces with several circle settings is done in minutes. Software checks each set against the others and flags a pointing that disagrees. Search for rounds of angles, electronic theodolite set collection and angular closure.
